points.en: Step Four asks what other people the counselee has already talked to, to gauge the seriousness of the problem and spot a pattern of moving from helper to helper.
It leads to referral because the history can reveal the problem is beyond the pastor's competence, such as heavy professional or psychiatric involvement, and proceeding would do harm.
Inwardly he resists the pull to be the one who finally succeeds or to feel defensive, and recognizes the pattern of a wounded person who cannot settle with any helper.
Outwardly he gently names the pattern and asks what makes it hard to settle on one helper, without joining the complaint against the others.
He may predict the same thing could happen with him when he says what others said, and invite naming that possibility now.
Step Four shows he has sought no help, and suicidal thoughts are a category that warrants immediate referral beyond ordinary pastoral counseling.
He takes the disclosure seriously and refers promptly for medical and professional help, naming the referral with confidence as care rather than rejection.
The pastor stays involved after referral, praying and walking alongside as part of coordinated care.
The test is whether the matter is outside his competence or whether he is outside his courage, not whether it is hard.
Ordinary matters (marriage, grief, anxiety, sin, discouragement) stay pastoral; referral is for things like suicide gestures, serious addiction or chronic psychiatric illness.
Spiritual and clinical causes can look alike, so a seemingly spiritual problem may be clinical and long-treated depression may be spiritual.
Proverbs 11:14 teaches that safety lies in many counselors, so the pastor is not meant to be the sole helper and need not solve everything himself.
This supports investigating other helpers and referring or coordinating care, since professional help and pastoral help work together.
He asks what the earlier counseling gave and what the counselee wanted and did not receive, to tell a genuine mismatch from a pattern of leaving when responsibility comes up.
He honors the previous counselor without disparaging him and stays open to coordinating with that helper.
Admitting limits is humility: the pastor is not the savior or an omnipotent fixer, and Christ alone heals.
Referring well is an act of love that gets the counselee the best help while the pastor keeps walking with him spiritually.
The claim is critiqued because referral is often pastoral wisdom when a problem exceeds competence, and a good referral is care that continues pastoral support.
The opposite error is premature referral of ordinary pastoral matters, which is cowardice, treating the office as a switchboard.
The pattern of previous helpers is itself diagnostic information that can reveal the real problem faster than the counselee's own account.
An example is the counselee who left many helpers once the conversation turned to his own responsibility, showing that avoidance of responsibility is the issue.
Disparaging a previous counselor teaches the counselee that pastors speak ill of one another and that he would be treated the same, so he becomes less open.
The pastor models honor for absent helpers, redirecting to what the counselee needed, and names real harm without contempt.
